## Overview

These are the materials for the lectures and workshop prepared for 
the visit to the University of Pavia in the framework of the 
**HerIT4future** project.

## Description 

Vector-borne and zoonotic diseases impose a significant burden on human health worldwide, and their dyamics are tightly coupled to environmental conditions that can be monitored from space. This series of lectures, seminars and workshops explore the intersection of remote sensing and disease ecology, addressing both the conceptual foundations and the methodological challenges of building operational disease surveillance tools from satellite data. 
We begin with the theoretical framework linking remote sensing to health geography and disease ecology, illustrated through case studies spanning hantavirus, dengue, leishmaniasis and West Nile fever. A research seminar then dissects a real analytical pipeline, combining field ovitrap time series, unsupervised clustering and machine learning with Sentinel-2 imagery, to map Aedes aegypti temporal activity across an entire city and validate predictions against dengue incidence. A hands-on workshop guides participants through a complete species distribution modeling workflow with GRASS and Python within Jupyter notebooks and Google Colab, from satellite data to spatially explicit distribution maps. The series closes with a collaborative problem-solving session, where open methodological challenges in RS-based disease surveillance, such as sparse data, class imbalance, model transferability, are brought to the table for collective discussion.
Across all sessions, the emphasis is on reproducibility, open-source tools, and the translation of RS data into actionable public health information.
